reminder: A compact core of a 3-manifold is a [compact](c:compact-space) [submanifold](c:submanifold) that carries the whole [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group).
definition: Let $M$ be a connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold). A compact core of $M$ is a connected [compact](c:compact-space) 3-dimensional [submanifold](c:submanifold) $C\subseteq M$ such that the inclusion $C\to M$ induces an isomorphism of [fundamental groups](c:fundamental-group).
examples: For $M=\mathbb{R}^3$ every closed ball is a compact core, because both fundamental groups are trivial.
For $M=S^1\times\mathbb{R}^2$ the solid torus $S^1\times D^2$ is a compact core.
A finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold has a compact core: remove an open neighbourhood of each cusp.
Non-example: a small ball in $S^1\times\mathbb{R}^2$ is compact, but its inclusion kills the fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}$ of $M$, so it is not a core.

reminder: In a compact extension, the functions that are almost periodic over the base span a dense part of all functions.
definition: Let $X\to Y$ be an extension of [measure-preserving systems](c:measure-preserving-system) with transformation $T$. A function $f\in L^2(X)$ is almost periodic over $Y$ when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, finitely many functions $g_1,\dots,g_k$ exist such that every translate $T^nf$ lies within $\varepsilon$ of some $g_i$ in the relative norm $\mathbb{E}(|h|^2\mid Y)^{1/2}$, defined with [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation), at almost every point of $Y$. The extension is compact when such functions span a dense subspace of $L^2(X)$.
examples: The skew product $T(x,y)=(x+\alpha,\,y+x)$ on the torus $\mathbb{T}^2$ is a compact extension of the rotation $x\mapsto x+\alpha$ of the circle.
Every isometric extension, that is every extension by a compact group, is compact.
Non-example: the projection $Y\times Z\to Y$ with $Z$ a non-trivial weakly mixing system is not compact, because only functions of $y$ alone are almost periodic over $Y$.

reminder: A semisimple real Lie algebra is compact when its [Killing form](c:killing-form) is negative definite.
definition: A [semisimple](c:is-semisimple) real [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ is compact when its [Killing form](c:killing-form) $B(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\,\operatorname{ad}y)$ is a negative [definite](c:definite-form) [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form). Equivalently, $\mathfrak{g}$ is the Lie algebra of a [compact Lie group](c:compact-lie-group).
examples: $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is compact: in the basis $i\sigma_k/2$, with $\sigma_k$ the Pauli matrices, its Killing form is $-2$ times the standard inner product.
$\mathfrak{so}(n)$ for $n\ge3$ and $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ for $n\ge2$ are compact.
Non-example: $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ is semisimple, but its Killing form has $B(h,h)=8>0$ for $h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, so it is not negative definite.

steps: Start with a compact Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, which is semisimple by definition.
So $\mathfrak{g}$ is a [semisimple Lie algebra](c:is-semisimple), and its Killing form is non-degenerate.
The compact case adds one condition: the Killing form is negative definite, not just non-degenerate.
links.why: It shows that compactness is a sign condition on the Killing form of a semisimple Lie algebra.

reminder: The compact-open topology on continuous maps has as subbase the maps that send a [compact](c:compact-subspace) set into an [open set](c:open-set).
definition: For [topological spaces](c:topological-space) $X$ and $Y$, the compact-open topology on the set $C(X,Y)$ of [continuous maps](c:continuous-function) has as subbase the sets $V(K,U)=\{f : f(K)\subseteq U\}$, where $K\subseteq X$ is a [compact subspace](c:compact-subspace) and $U\subseteq Y$ is an [open set](c:open-set). A basic open set is a finite intersection of such sets.
examples: If $X$ is a point, then $C(X,Y)$ is $Y$ itself, and the compact-open topology is the topology of $Y$.
If $Y$ is a metric space, the compact-open topology is the topology of [uniform convergence](c:uniform-convergence) on compact sets.
Non-example: the topology of pointwise convergence on $C(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ is different, because the bumps $f_n(x)=\max(0,1-n|x-1/n|)$ tend to $0$ pointwise but not uniformly on $[0,1]$.

reminder: For an [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor), the comparison functor sends each object to an [algebra](c:algebra-over-a-monad) over the induced [monad](c:monad).
definition: Let $F\dashv U$ be an [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor) with $U:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ and counit $\varepsilon$, and let $T=UF$ be the induced [monad](c:monad) on $\mathcal{D}$. The comparison functor $K:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}^T$ sends an object $c$ to the [algebra over the monad](c:algebra-over-a-monad) $(Uc,\,U\varepsilon_c)$ in the [Eilenberg-Moore category](c:eilenberg-moore-category) $\mathcal{D}^T$. It is the unique functor with $U^TK=U$ and $KF=F^T$, where $F^T\dashv U^T$ is the free-forgetful adjunction of $T$.
examples: For the free-forgetful adjunction between sets and groups, $K$ is an equivalence from groups to algebras of the free-group monad, so the adjunction is [monadic](c:monadic-adjunction).
For the adjunction between discrete spaces and the forgetful functor $U:\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Set}$, the monad is the identity monad, so $K=U$, which is not an equivalence.
Non-example: a functor $G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}^T$ with $U^TG\ne U$ is not the comparison functor, because $K$ must commute with the two forgetful functors.

reminder: A compass and straightedge construction builds new points from given points by drawing only [lines](c:line) and [circles](c:circle).
definition: Start with a set of given points in the plane. A step draws the [line](c:line) through two known points, or the [circle](c:circle) with a known centre that passes through another known point, and adds each intersection of two drawn curves as a new known point. A construction is a finite sequence of such steps.
examples: Two circles, each centred at one end of a segment and passing through the other end, meet in two points; the line through them is the perpendicular bisector of the segment.
The same two circles also give the third vertex of an equilateral triangle on the segment.
Gauss constructed the regular 17-gon in this way.
Non-example: a step that marks two points on the straightedge (a neusis) is not allowed, so a neusis trisection of an angle is not a compass and straightedge construction.

reminder: A variety $X$ is complete when each projection $X\times Y\to Y$ is a [closed map](c:closed-map).
definition: An [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) $X$ over a field $k$ (separated by definition) is complete when, for every variety $Y$ over $k$, the projection $X\times Y\to Y$ is a [closed map](c:closed-map) in the Zariski topology. Equivalently, the structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is [universally closed](c:universally-closed).
examples: Every projective variety is complete, for example projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$.
A variety over $\mathbb{C}$ is complete exactly when it is compact in the classical topology.

Non-example: the affine line $\mathbb{A}^1$ is not complete, because the projection of the closed hyperbola $\{xy=1\}\subset\mathbb{A}^1\times\mathbb{A}^1$ to the first factor is $\mathbb{A}^1\setminus\{0\}$, which is not closed.

steps: Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{P}^n$ be a [projective variety](c:projective-variety) and let $Y$ be any variety.
The projection $\mathbb{P}^n\times Y\to Y$ is a closed map, because projective space is complete.
The product $X\times Y$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{P}^n\times Y$, so the restricted projection $X\times Y\to Y$ is also closed.
Hence $X$ is complete; the converse fails in general, because a complete variety need not be projective.
links.why: It shows that completeness is the intrinsic part of projectivity, with no embedding in projective space.

reminder: Completing the square writes a quadratic polynomial as a constant times a square plus a constant.
definition: Let $K$ be a [field](c:field) in which $2\ne0$. For $a\ne0$, completing the square rewrites the quadratic [polynomial](c:polynomial) $ax^2+bx+c$ as $a\bigl(x+\tfrac{b}{2a}\bigr)^2+\bigl(c-\tfrac{b^2}{4a}\bigr)$, so that $x$ occurs in one square only.
examples: The equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$ becomes $\bigl(x+\tfrac{b}{2a}\bigr)^2=\tfrac{b^2-4ac}{4a^2}$, which gives the quadratic formula.
Non-example: writing $x^2+6x+5$ as $(x+3)^2$ drops the constant $-4$, so the two expressions are not equal.

reminder: Complex cobordism is the [cohomology theory](c:generalized-cohomology) represented by the [Thom spectrum](c:thom-spectrum) $MU$ of complex vector bundles.
definition: Complex cobordism is the [generalized cohomology](c:generalized-cohomology) theory $MU^*$ represented by the [Thom spectrum](c:thom-spectrum) $MU$ of the universal [complex vector bundles](c:complex-vector-bundle), so that $MU^n(X)=[X,\Sigma^nMU]$. Its coefficient group $\pi_nMU$ is the group of [cobordism](c:cobordism) classes of closed stably complex $n$-manifolds.
examples: The coefficient ring $\pi_*MU$ is a polynomial ring on generators $x_i$ of degree $2i$.
$\pi_2MU\cong\mathbb{Z}$, generated by the class of $\mathbb{CP}^1$.
Non-example: unoriented cobordism $MO$ is not $MU$, because $\pi_*MO$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$ while $\pi_*MU$ has no torsion.

steps: Take the [cobordism](c:cobordism) relation on closed $n$-manifolds equipped with a chosen structure on the stable tangent bundle.
Choose a stable complex structure on the tangent bundle as this structure.
The cobordism classes of such manifolds form the coefficient groups $\pi_nMU$ of complex cobordism.
links.why: It shows that complex cobordism is cobordism of manifolds with one specific tangent structure.

steps: Take the Thom spectrum $MU$ of the universal complex bundles over $BU$.
The Thom class of the universal line bundle gives a class in $MU^2(\mathbb{CP}^\infty)$ that restricts to the generator on $\mathbb{CP}^1$.
Such a class is a complex orientation, so $MU$ is a [complex oriented cohomology theory](c:complex-oriented-cohomology-theory).
It is the universal one: each complex orientation of a ring spectrum $E$ comes from a ring map $MU\to E$.
links.why: It shows that $MU$ is the universal example, which is why results about complex oriented theories start from it.

reminder: A complex torus is the quotient of $\mathbb{C}^n$ by a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) of rank $2n$.
definition: A complex torus of dimension $n$ is a quotient $V/\Lambda$, where $V\cong\mathbb{C}^n$ is a complex [vector space](c:vector-space) and $\Lambda\subset V$ is a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup), that is a discrete subgroup of rank $2n$ that spans $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$. It is a compact connected [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) and a commutative group.
examples: $\mathbb{C}/(\mathbb{Z}+i\mathbb{Z})$ is a complex torus of dimension $1$.
$\mathbb{C}^n/(\mathbb{Z}^n+i\mathbb{Z}^n)$ is a complex torus of dimension $n$, a product of $n$ copies of the previous example.
Non-example: $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$ is a cylinder, because the subgroup $\mathbb{Z}$ has rank $1$ instead of $2$, so the quotient is not compact.
Non-example: $\mathbb{C}/(\mathbb{Z}+\sqrt2\,\mathbb{Z})$ is not a torus, because $\mathbb{Z}+\sqrt2\,\mathbb{Z}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, not discrete.

steps: Let $A$ be an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) over $\mathbb{C}$ of dimension $g$.
The group $A(\mathbb{C})$ is a compact connected commutative complex Lie group.
Its exponential map is a surjective homomorphism $\mathbb{C}^g\to A(\mathbb{C})$ whose kernel is a lattice $\Lambda$ of rank $2g$.
So $A(\mathbb{C})\cong\mathbb{C}^g/\Lambda$ is a complex torus; the abelian variety case adds a Riemann form on $\Lambda$, which makes the torus projective.
links.why: It shows that an abelian variety is a complex torus plus a polarization condition.

steps: Start with an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) $E$ over $\mathbb{C}$.
By uniformization, $E\cong\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ for a lattice $\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}\omega_1+\mathbb{Z}\omega_2$ of rank $2$.
So $E$ is a complex torus of dimension $1$.
Every complex torus of dimension $1$ arises this way, so the elliptic curve case adds no further condition than dimension $1$.
links.why: It shows that complex elliptic curves are exactly the one-dimensional complex tori.

reminder: A complex vector bundle is a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) whose fibres are complex vector spaces, glued by complex linear maps.
definition: A complex [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of rank $n$ over a space $B$ is a continuous map $\pi:E\to B$ such that each fibre $\pi^{-1}(b)$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) over $\mathbb{C}$, and each point of $B$ has a neighbourhood $U$ with a homeomorphism $\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times\mathbb{C}^n$ that is complex linear on every fibre. Equivalently, it is a [real vector bundle](c:real-vector-bundle) of rank $2n$ with a fibrewise [complex structure](c:complex-structure).
examples: The tautological line bundle over $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is a complex vector bundle of rank $1$.
The tangent bundle of a complex manifold is a complex vector bundle.
The trivial bundle $B\times\mathbb{C}^n$ is a complex vector bundle.
Non-example: the Möbius line bundle over the circle has fibres $\mathbb{R}$, which are not complex vector spaces.

steps: Let $E\to B$ be a complex vector bundle of rank $n$.
Forget the multiplication by $i$ and keep only real scalars.
Each fibre $\mathbb{C}^n$ is then a real vector space of dimension $2n$, and the local trivialisations stay linear over $\mathbb{R}$.
So $E$ is a [real vector bundle](c:real-vector-bundle) of rank $2n$; the complex case adds a fibrewise map $J$ with $J^2=-1$.
links.why: It shows that a complex structure on a bundle is extra data on a real bundle.

steps: Take a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle), whose total space is a complex manifold.
Its local trivialisations are biholomorphic and complex linear on each fibre.
Forget the holomorphic structure and keep only continuity of the trivialisations.
The result is a complex vector bundle; the holomorphic case adds that the transition functions are holomorphic.
links.why: It shows that holomorphic bundles are complex bundles with holomorphic transition functions.

reminder: The complexification of a [real vector space](c:real-vector-space) is its [tensor product](c:tensor-product) with the complex numbers.
definition: The complexification of a [real vector space](c:real-vector-space) $V$ is $V_{\mathbb{C}}=\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}V$, a [vector space](c:vector-space) over $\mathbb{C}$ with $\lambda\cdot(z\otimes v)=\lambda z\otimes v$. Each element of $V_{\mathbb{C}}$ is $v+iw$ for unique $v,w\in V$, and a real basis of $V$ is a complex basis of $V_{\mathbb{C}}$.
examples: The complexification of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $\mathbb{C}^n$.
The complexification of the space of real $n\times n$ matrices is the space of complex $n\times n$ matrices.
The complexification of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ is $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$.
Non-example: the complex line $\mathbb{C}$ is not its own complexification when viewed as the real plane; that real plane has complexification $\mathbb{C}^2$.

steps: Take the inclusion of rings $\mathbb{R}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$.
[Extension of scalars](c:extension-of-scalars) along it sends an $\mathbb{R}$-module $V$ to the $\mathbb{C}$-module $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}V$.
For a real vector space $V$, this module is the complexification of $V$.
So complexification is extension of scalars for the single inclusion $\mathbb{R}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$.
links.why: It shows that general facts about extension of scalars, such as the universal property, apply to complexification.

reminder: [Composition](c:composition) in a [category](c:category) turns morphisms $f:x\to y$ and $g:y\to z$ into one morphism $g\circ f:x\to z$.
definition: In a [category](c:category), composition assigns to each pair of morphisms $f:x\to y$ and $g:y\to z$, where the target of $f$ is the source of $g$, a composite $g\circ f:x\to z$. It is [associative](c:associativity), $h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f$, and each object $x$ has an identity $\mathrm{id}_x$ with $f\circ\mathrm{id}_x=f=\mathrm{id}_y\circ f$.
examples: In the category of sets, $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$.
In the category of vector spaces, composition of linear maps is multiplication of matrices.
In a partially ordered set viewed as a category, composition is transitivity: $a\le b$ and $b\le c$ give $a\le c$.
Non-example: the maps $f:A\to B$ and $g:C\to D$ with $B\ne C$ have no composite in the category of sets, because the target of $f$ is not the source of $g$.

reminder: A computable metric space is a [metric space](c:metric-space) with a [dense](c:dense-set) sequence whose distances are uniformly [computable](c:computable-real-number).
definition: A computable metric space is a triple $(X,d,s)$ where $(X,d)$ is a [metric space](c:metric-space) and $s=(s_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence that is [dense](c:dense-set) in $X$. The distances $d(s_i,s_j)$ must be [computable real numbers](c:computable-real-number) uniformly in $i$ and $j$, that is, one algorithm computes each of them to any precision. Usually $X$ is also complete.
examples: The real line with $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ and a computable enumeration of the rationals is a computable metric space.
Cantor space $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with $d(x,y)=2^{-n}$, where $n$ is the first place that $x$ and $y$ differ, and the eventually-zero sequences as ideal points, is a computable metric space.
Non-example: the real line with a dense sequence whose first two terms are a non-computable real $a$ and $0$ fails, because $d(s_0,s_1)=|a|$ is not computable.

steps: Let $(X,d,s)$ be a computable metric space.
The sequence $s$ is a countable dense subset of $X$.
So $X$ is a [separable metric space](c:separable-metric-space).
The computable case adds that the distances between the chosen dense points are computable uniformly.
links.why: It shows that computable metric spaces are separable metric spaces with extra computability data.

reminder: A concatenated code encodes a message with an outer code, and then encodes each outer symbol with an inner code.
definition: Let the inner code encode $\mathbb{F}_q^k$ into $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, and let the outer code have length $N$ over the alphabet $\mathbb{F}_{q^k}\cong\mathbb{F}_q^k$, where $\mathbb{F}_q$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field). The concatenated code maps a message to an outer codeword $(c_1,\dots,c_N)$ and replaces each symbol $c_j$ by its inner codeword, which gives a word of length $nN$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. If the two codes have minimum distances $d$ and $D$, the concatenated code has minimum distance at least $dD$.
examples: The binary [Hamming code](c:hamming-code) $[7,4,3]$ as inner code and a Reed-Solomon code $[15,11,5]$ over $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ as outer code give a binary $[105,44,\ge15]$ code.
In the threshold theorem, a quantum code such as the Steane code $[[7,1,3]]$ is concatenated with itself $l$ times to give a code with distance at least $3^l$.
Non-example: a product code puts the message in an array and encodes rows and columns, but no inner code acts on the symbols of one outer codeword, so it is not a concatenation.

reminder: A conformal field theory is a quantum field theory that has the [conformal group](c:conformal-group) among its symmetries.
definition: In its functorial form, a conformal field theory is a [functorial field theory](c:functorial-field-theory) on the [conformal cobordism category](c:conformal-cobordism-category): it assigns a vector space to each closed manifold with a conformal structure and a linear map to each conformal cobordism, compatibly with gluing. A conformal rescaling of the metric changes the maps only by an anomaly factor that the [central charge](c:central-charge) controls.
examples: The free massless boson in two dimensions is a conformal field theory with central charge $1$.
The Ising model at its critical point is a two-dimensional conformal field theory with central charge $1/2$.
Non-example: the free scalar field with mass $m>0$ is not conformal, because the mass sets a length scale, so rescaling the metric changes the theory.

steps: Take the cobordism category whose objects are closed manifolds and whose morphisms are cobordisms.
Equip each manifold and cobordism with a conformal structure, which gives the [conformal cobordism category](c:conformal-cobordism-category).
A [functorial field theory](c:functorial-field-theory) on this category is a conformal field theory, up to the anomaly of the central charge.
links.why: It shows that a conformal field theory is a field theory whose geometry is conformal instead of metric.

steps: Start with a conformal field theory in dimension two, with Virasoro symmetry of central charge $c$.
Add the conditions that the Virasoro algebra is the whole chiral symmetry and that only finitely many primary fields occur.
Such theories are the Virasoro [minimal models](c:minimal-model-cft), labelled by coprime integers $p,q\ge2$ with $c=1-6(p-q)^2/(pq)$.
links.why: It shows that minimal models are the two-dimensional conformal field theories with finitely many Virasoro primary fields.

reminder: A conformal manifold is a manifold with a conformal class of metrics, which fixes angles but not lengths.
definition: A conformal manifold is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ with a conformal class $[g]=\{e^{2f}g : f\in C^\infty(M)\}$ of a [Riemannian metric](c:riemannian-manifold) $g$; the class is an [equivalence class](c:equivalence-class) of metrics that differ by a positive function. Two metrics in the same class give the same angles between tangent vectors but different lengths.
examples: Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the class of the standard metric is a conformal manifold.
The round sphere $S^n$ is conformally equivalent to $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a point added, by stereographic projection.
On an oriented surface, a conformal structure is the same as a complex structure, so a Riemann surface is a conformal manifold.
Non-example: on $\mathbb{R}^2$ the metrics $dx^2+dy^2$ and $dx^2+4\,dy^2$ are not conformally related, because they stretch lengths differently in different directions and change angles.

steps: At each point, collect the frames of the tangent space that are orthonormal up to scale for some metric in the class.
These frames form a principal bundle with structure group $CO(n)=\mathbb{R}_{>0}\times O(n)$.
A reduction of the frame bundle to $CO(n)$ is a [G-structure](c:g-structure) with $G=CO(n)$.
So a conformal structure is exactly a $G$-structure for this group.
links.why: It shows that conformal geometry is the geometry of $CO(n)$-structures.

reminder: A positive rational number is congruent when it is the [area](c:area) of a [right triangle](c:right-triangle) with rational sides.
definition: A positive [rational number](c:rational-number) $n$ is congruent when a [right triangle](c:right-triangle) with rational side lengths $a$, $b$, $c$ and $a^2+b^2=c^2$ has [area](c:area) $ab/2=n$. Equivalently, the elliptic curve $y^2=x^3-n^2x$ has a rational point with $y\ne0$.
examples: $6$ is congruent: the triangle with sides $3,4,5$ has area $6$.
$5$ is congruent: the triangle with sides $3/2,\,20/3,\,41/6$ has area $5$.
Non-example: $1$ is not congruent, because no right triangle with rational sides has area $1$ (Fermat, by descent).

reminder: Two [subgroups](c:subgroup) $H_1$ and $H_2$ of $G$ are conjugate when $gH_1g^{-1}=H_2$ for some $g\in G$.
definition: Subgroups $H_1$ and $H_2$ of a [group](c:group) $G$ are conjugate subgroups when some $g\in G$ satisfies $gH_1g^{-1}=H_2$, that is, when the [conjugation action](c:conjugation-action) of $g$ maps $H_1$ onto $H_2$. This is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) on the set of subgroups of $G$.
examples: In $S_3$ the subgroups $\langle(1\,2)\rangle$ and $\langle(1\,3)\rangle$ are conjugate, because conjugation by $(2\,3)$ maps $(1\,2)$ to $(1\,3)$.
All Sylow $p$-subgroups of a finite group are conjugate to each other.
Non-example: in an abelian group $gHg^{-1}=H$ for all $g$, so two different subgroups are never conjugate.

reminder: A filtered space is connected when each pair $(X_j,X_i)$ with $i<j$ is $i$-connected.
definition: A filtered space is a space with subspaces $X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq X_2\subseteq\cdots$. It is connected when, for all $0\le i<j$, the pair $(X_j,X_i)$ is $i$-connected, that is $\pi_k(X_j,X_i,v)=0$ for $0\le k\le i$ and every base point $v\in X_0$ (for $k=0$ this says that each path component of $X_j$ meets $X_i$). Here $\pi_k$ denotes the relative [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group).
examples: The skeletal filtration $X_i=X^{(i)}$ of a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) is connected, by cellular approximation.
The constant filtration $X_i=X$ of any space is connected when $X_0=X$ has the base points in every path component.
Non-example: the filtration $X_0=\{p\}\subset X_1=\{p,q\}$ of a two-point space is not connected, because the path component of $q$ does not meet $X_0$.

reminder: The connected sum of two $n$-manifolds removes an open [ball](c:ball) from each and glues the two boundary spheres together.
definition: For connected $n$-[manifolds](c:manifold) $M$ and $N$, remove an open [ball](c:ball) from each and glue the remaining pieces along their [boundary](c:boundary) spheres by a diffeomorphism, which reverses orientation when $M$ and $N$ are oriented. The result is the connected sum $M\#N$. More generally, one removes tubular neighbourhoods of a common [submanifold](c:submanifold) and glues along their boundaries.
examples: $T^2\#T^2$ is the closed orientable surface of genus $2$.
$\mathbb{RP}^2\#\mathbb{RP}^2$ is the Klein bottle, and $M\#S^n\cong M$ for every $n$-manifold $M$.
Non-example: the wedge sum $M\vee N$ identifies one point of each manifold, and it is not a manifold, because the wedge point has no neighbourhood that is a ball.

reminder: A connection differentiates sections of a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) by an operator that obeys the Leibniz rule.
definition:
A connection on a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E	o M$ over a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear map $
abla$ from sections of $E$ to $E$-valued [1-forms](c:differential-form) with $
abla(fs)=df\otimes s+f
abla s$ for every smooth function $f$ and section $s$. For a [vector field](c:vector-field) $X$, the covariant derivative $
abla_Xs$ measures how $s$ changes along $X$, and the [curvature](c:curvature) measures how parallel transport around small loops fails to be trivial.
examples: On the trivial bundle $M\times\mathbb{R}^k$, the rule $\nabla s=ds$ is a connection.
The Levi-Civita connection is a connection on the tangent bundle of a Riemannian manifold.
Non-example: the Lie derivative $X\mapsto\mathcal{L}_XY$ is not a connection, because $\mathcal{L}_{fX}Y=f\mathcal{L}_XY-Y(f)X$ is not linear over functions in $X$.

steps: Take a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(M,g)$ and the vector bundle $TM$.
Choose a connection $\nabla$ on $TM$ with $\nabla g=0$, so parallel transport keeps lengths and angles.
Require also that $\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$, so the torsion vanishes.
Exactly one connection meets both conditions; it is the [Levi-Civita connection](c:levi-civita-connection).
links.why: It shows that the Levi-Civita connection is the connection on $TM$ that is compatible with the metric and torsion-free.

reminder: The constant term of a [polynomial](c:polynomial) is the coefficient of the monomial of degree zero.
definition: For a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p=\sum_k a_kx^k$ in one variable, the constant term is $a_0=p(0)$. For a [Laurent polynomial](c:laurent-polynomial) in several variables, it is the coefficient of the monomial $1$.
examples: The constant term of $3x^2-5x+7$ is $7$.
Dyson's identity says that the constant term of $\prod_{i\ne j}(1-x_i/x_j)^{a_i}$ is $\frac{(a_1+\cdots+a_n)!}{a_1!\cdots a_n!}$.
Non-example: $p(1)$ is the sum of all coefficients of $p$, not its constant term.

reminder: A constructible set is a finite union of [locally closed sets](c:locally-closed-set) in a Noetherian space.
definition: In a Noetherian [topological space](c:topological-space), such as the Zariski spectrum of a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring), a subset is constructible when it is a finite union of [locally closed sets](c:locally-closed-set), each of the form $U\cap Z$ with $U$ [open](c:open-set) and $Z$ [closed](c:closed-set). Equivalently, it belongs to the [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) of subsets generated by the open sets.
examples: In $\mathbb{A}^2$ the set $\{x\ne0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}$ is constructible, and it is neither open nor closed; it is the image of $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$.
Chevalley's theorem says that the image of a constructible set under a morphism of finite presentation is constructible.
Non-example: the integers $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{A}^1(\mathbb{C})$ are not constructible, because a constructible subset of the affine line is finite or has a finite complement.

steps: Let $S=U\cap Z$ be a [locally closed set](c:locally-closed-set), with $U$ open and $Z$ closed.
Then $S$ is a finite union of locally closed sets, with only one set in the union.
So every locally closed set is constructible, and so are all open sets and all closed sets.
The constructible case adds finite unions, and hence complements and finite intersections.
links.why: It shows that constructible sets are the sets built from locally closed sets by finite Boolean operations.

reminder: The constructible universe is the class of sets that appear in stages of repeated taking of [definable](c:definable-set) subsets.
definition: By [transfinite induction](c:transfinite-induction) on [ordinals](c:ordinal), let $L_0=\emptyset$, let $L_{\alpha+1}$ be the set of subsets of $L_\alpha$ that are [definable](c:definable-set) with parameters in $(L_\alpha,\in)$, and let $L_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}L_\alpha$ for a limit ordinal $\lambda$. The constructible universe is the class $L=\bigcup_\alpha L_\alpha$.
examples: Every ordinal belongs to $L$, and $L_\alpha\cap\mathrm{Ord}=\alpha$.
$L_\omega$ is the set of hereditarily finite sets.
Gödel showed that $L$ satisfies [ZFC](c:zfc) and the continuum hypothesis.
Non-example: a subset of $\omega$ added by [forcing](c:forcing) over $L$, a Cohen real, is not in $L$.

reminder: Two function germs are contact equivalent when a change of coordinates and a unit factor turn one into the other.
definition: Two [germs](c:germ) of [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) $f,g:(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ are contact equivalent when there are a germ of [biholomorphic map](c:biholomorphic-function) $\varphi$ of $(\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ and a unit $u$ of the [local ring](c:local-ring) $\mathcal{O}_n$ with $g=u\cdot(f\circ\varphi)$. For map germs to $\mathbb{C}^p$, the unit $u$ becomes a germ of invertible $p\times p$ matrices. This is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation), and it keeps the local ring $\mathcal{O}_n/(f)$ up to isomorphism.
examples: $x^2+y^2$ and $xy$ are contact equivalent: the linear change $X=x+iy$, $Y=x-iy$ turns $x^2+y^2$ into $XY$.
A germ $f$ and $(1+x)f$ are contact equivalent, with $\varphi$ the identity and the unit $u=1+x$.
Non-example: $x^2+y^2$ and $x^3+y^2$ are not contact equivalent, because their Tjurina numbers $\dim\mathcal{O}_2/(f,f_x,f_y)$ are $1$ and $2$.

reminder: The continuity equation says that the density of a conserved quantity changes only through its flux.
definition:
For a density $ho(x,t)$ and a [vector field](c:vector-field) $v$ of velocities, the continuity equation is $\partial_tho+
abla\cdot(ho v)=0$, where $
abla\cdot$ is the divergence and $\partial_t$ is a [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative). More generally, $\partial_tho+
abla\cdot J=0$ for a flux $J$. It says that the integral of $ho$ over a region changes only by the flux of $J$ across the boundary of the region.
examples: Conservation of mass in a fluid with density $\rho$ and velocity $v$ is the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=0$.
Liouville's equation for a phase-space density that moves with a flow $\dot x$ is $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\dot x)=0$.
The heat equation $\partial_tu=\Delta u$ is a continuity equation with flux $J=-\nabla u$.
Non-example: $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=s$ with a source $s\ne0$ is not a continuity equation, because it does not conserve the total mass.

steps: A [conservation law](c:conservation-law) says that the total of a quantity in a region changes only by what crosses the boundary.
Take a quantity with density $\rho$ and flux $J$.
By the divergence theorem, the rate of change of the content of a region $\Omega$ is minus the flux of $J$ through $\partial\Omega$.
This holds for every small region, so $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot J=0$ at each point.
links.why: It shows that the continuity equation is the local, differential form of a conservation law.

reminder: A continuous functional calculus turns each [continuous](c:continuous-function) function $f$ on the [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) of $a$ into an element $f(a)$.
definition: Let $A$ be a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) and $a\in A$. A continuous functional calculus for $a$ is a $*$-homomorphism $C(\sigma(a))\to A$, written $f\mapsto f(a)$, that sends the identity function $z\mapsto z$ on the [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) $\sigma(a)$ to $a$. It exists, and is unique, exactly when $a$ is [normal](c:normal-operator).
examples: For a normal matrix $a=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)U^*$, the calculus gives $f(a)=U\operatorname{diag}(f(\lambda_1),\dots,f(\lambda_n))U^*$.
For a positive element $a$ of a C*-algebra, $f=\sqrt{\cdot}$ gives the square root $\sqrt a$, and $f=\exp$ gives $e^a$.

Non-example: the nilpotent matrix $a=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is not normal and has no such calculus, because $\sigma(a)=\{0\}$ and the identity function on $\{0\}$ is $0$, so it would map to $0\ne a$.

steps: A [functional calculus](c:functional-calculus) for $a$ is an algebra map from a space of functions on $\sigma(a)$ to $A$ that sends the identity function to $a$.
Choose the algebra $C(\sigma(a))$ of continuous functions as the space of functions.
Require the map to respect the star operation, so that $\bar f$ goes to $f(a)^*$.
For a normal element, this map exists and is the continuous functional calculus.
links.why: It shows that the continuous functional calculus is the functional calculus for continuous functions that respects the adjoint.

reminder: A contravariant functor sends a morphism $f:x\to y$ to a morphism $F(y)\to F(x)$ and reverses composition.
definition: A contravariant functor $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ between [categories](c:category) assigns an object $F(x)$ to each object $x$ and a morphism $F(f):F(y)\to F(x)$ to each morphism $f:x\to y$, so that $F(\mathrm{id}_x)=\mathrm{id}_{F(x)}$ and $F(g\circ f)=F(f)\circ F(g)$. Equivalently, it is a [functor](c:functor) from the [opposite category](c:opposite-category) $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}$ to $\mathcal{D}$.
examples: The dual space $V\mapsto V^*$ with $f\mapsto f^*$ is a contravariant functor on vector spaces.
The power set $X\mapsto\mathcal{P}(X)$ with $f\mapsto f^{-1}$ is a contravariant functor on sets.
For each object $A$, the functor $\operatorname{Hom}(-,A)$ is contravariant.
Non-example: the forgetful functor from groups to sets keeps the direction of each map, so it is covariant and not contravariant.

steps: Let $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ be a contravariant functor.
Form the [opposite category](c:opposite-category) $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}$, with the same objects and all arrows reversed.
Define $F':\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal{D}$ by $F'(x)=F(x)$ and $F'(f^{\mathrm{op}})=F(f)$.
Then $F'$ keeps identities and composition, so it is an ordinary [functor](c:functor).
links.why: It shows that every result about functors applies to contravariant functors on the opposite category.

steps: Start with a contravariant functor $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbf{Set}$.
It sends each object $x$ to a set $F(x)$ and each morphism $f:x\to y$ to a map $F(y)\to F(x)$.
This data is by definition a [presheaf](c:presheaf) on $\mathcal{C}$.
A general contravariant functor may have values in any category, and the presheaf case adds that the values are sets.
links.why: It shows that a presheaf is a contravariant functor with values in sets.

reminder: A control-flow graph has a node for each block of straight-line code and an edge for each possible jump.
definition: The control-flow graph of a [program](c:program) is a [directed graph](c:directed-graph) whose nodes are the basic blocks, which are maximal runs of instructions with one entry at the start and one exit at the end. It has an edge from block $A$ to block $B$ when execution can pass from the end of $A$ to the start of $B$, and it marks one entry node and the exit nodes.
examples: An if-then-else gives a diamond: a test node with an edge to the then-block and an edge to the else-block, and both blocks have an edge to the join node.
A while loop gives a test node with an edge into the body and a back edge from the body to the test.
Non-example: a call graph has a node for each procedure and an edge for each call, so it does not show the jumps inside a procedure.

steps: Take the basic blocks of a program as the vertices.
Draw an edge $A\to B$ when control can pass from $A$ to $B$.
These vertices and edges form a [directed graph](c:directed-graph).
The control-flow case adds an entry node, and the meaning of the edges as possible jumps.
links.why: It shows that graph results about reachability and cycles apply to the possible executions of a program.

reminder: The convex conjugate of $f$ at $y$ is the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) over $x$ of $\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)$.
definition: For a function $f:E\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}$ on an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) $E$, with values in the [extended real numbers](c:extended-real-number), the convex conjugate is $f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in E}\bigl(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)\bigr)$. It is a [convex function](c:convex-function) of $y$, whether or not $f$ is convex.
examples: For $f(x)=x^2/2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the conjugate is $f^*(y)=y^2/2$.
For $f(x)=|x|$, the conjugate is $0$ on $[-1,1]$ and $+\infty$ outside.
For $f(x)=e^x$, the conjugate is $f^*(y)=y\ln y-y$ for $y>0$.
Non-example: $g(y)=-y^2$ is not the conjugate of any function, because every convex conjugate is convex and $g$ is concave.

steps: Let $f$ be smooth and strictly convex, with $\nabla f$ a bijection.
The function $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)$ is concave and has its maximum where $\nabla f(x)=y$.
So $f^*(y)=\langle x_y,y\rangle-f(x_y)$ with $x_y=(\nabla f)^{-1}(y)$.
This is the [Legendre transform](c:legendre-transform) of $f$.
links.why: It shows that the convex conjugate extends the Legendre transform to functions that are not smooth or not strictly convex.

reminder: A convex polytope is the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of finitely many points in Euclidean space.
definition: A convex polytope in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of a finite set of points. Equivalently, it is a bounded intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces.
examples: The cube $[0,1]^n$, the regular octahedron and every simplex are convex polytopes.
A convex polygon is a convex polytope in the plane.
Non-example: the closed unit disk is convex, but it is not the convex hull of any finite set, so it is not a polytope.
Non-example: a closed half-plane is an intersection of finitely many half-spaces, but it is unbounded.

steps: A [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron) is an intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces.
A convex polytope is such an intersection that is also bounded.
So every convex polytope is a convex polyhedron.
The polytope case adds boundedness.
links.why: It shows that polytopes are exactly the bounded polyhedra.

steps: Take $n+1$ affinely independent points in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Their convex hull is a [simplex](c:simplex).
It is the convex hull of a finite set, so it is a convex polytope.
The simplex case adds that the generating points are affinely independent.
links.why: It shows that a simplex is the polytope with the fewest vertices in its dimension.

reminder: A cooperative game assigns to each coalition of players the total payoff that its members can secure together.
definition: A cooperative game with transferable utility is a pair $(N,v)$ of a [finite set](c:finite-set) $N$ of players and a [function](c:function) $v$ from the [power set](c:power-set) of $N$ to $\mathbb{R}$ with $v(\emptyset)=0$. The number $v(S)$ is the total payoff that the coalition $S\subseteq N$ can secure by acting together, and a solution divides $v(N)$ among the players.
examples: In the three-player majority game, $v(S)=1$ if $|S|\ge2$ and $v(S)=0$ otherwise.
In a glove game, $v(S)$ is the number of matched pairs of left and right gloves that the players in $S$ own together.
Non-example: the prisoner's dilemma in normal form lists payoffs for strategy choices and allows no binding agreements, so it has no function $v$ on coalitions.

reminder: A copresheaf on a [category](c:category) $\mathcal{C}$ is a [functor](c:functor) from $\mathcal{C}$ to sets.
definition: A copresheaf on a [category](c:category) $\mathcal{C}$ is a [functor](c:functor) $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbf{Set}$, that is, a [presheaf](c:presheaf) on the [opposite category](c:opposite-category) $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}$. It assigns a set $F(c)$ to each object and a map $F(f):F(c)\to F(d)$ to each morphism $f:c\to d$, and it respects identities and composition.
examples: For each object $c$, the representable functor $\operatorname{Hom}(c,-)$ is a copresheaf.
A $G$-set is a copresheaf on the category with one object and the morphisms given by the elements of $G$.

Non-example: $\operatorname{Hom}(-,c)$ sends $f:x\to y$ to a map $\operatorname{Hom}(y,c)\to\operatorname{Hom}(x,c)$ in the wrong direction, so it is a presheaf on $\mathcal{C}$ and not a copresheaf on $\mathcal{C}$.

steps: Let $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbf{Set}$ be a copresheaf.
By definition, $F$ is a [functor](c:functor) from $\mathcal{C}$ to the category of sets.
The copresheaf case adds that the target is the category of sets.
links.why: It shows that every result about functors applies to copresheaves.

steps: Let $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbf{Set}$ be a copresheaf.
The opposite of $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}$ is $\mathcal{C}$ again.
So $F$ is a functor $(\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}})^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$.
Hence $F$ is a [presheaf](c:presheaf) on $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}}$.
links.why: It shows that copresheaves on a category are the same as presheaves on its opposite.

reminder: The correlation of two [random variables](c:random-variable) is their covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations.
definition: For [random variables](c:random-variable) $X$ and $Y$ with positive finite [variance](c:variance), the correlation is $\rho(X,Y)=\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)$, where $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-EX)(Y-EY)]$ and $E$ is the [expected value](c:expected-value). It lies in $[-1,1]$, it is $\pm1$ exactly when $Y$ is an affine function of $X$, and it is $0$ when $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
examples: If $Y=2X+1$ with $X$ non-constant, then $\rho(X,Y)=1$.
For two outcomes $A,B\in\{-1,1\}$ with mean $0$, as in a Bell test, $\rho(A,B)=E[AB]$.
Non-example: the covariance is not the correlation, because $\mathrm{Cov}(10X,Y)=10\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$ but $\rho(10X,Y)=\rho(X,Y)$.

reminder: A set of coset representatives for $H$ in $G$ contains exactly one element of each [coset](c:coset) of $H$.
definition: Let $H$ be a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of a [group](c:group) $G$. A set of coset representatives, or transversal, is a subset $T\subseteq G$ that contains exactly one element of each left [coset](c:coset) $gH$, so that every $g\in G$ is $g=th$ in exactly one way with $t\in T$ and $h\in H$. For right cosets $Hg$ one asks the same.
examples: For $H=n\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Z}$, the set $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ is a set of coset representatives.
For $H=A_n$ in $S_n$ with $n\ge2$, the set $\{e,(1\,2)\}$ is a set of coset representatives.
Non-example: for $H=2\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Z}$, the set $\{0,2\}$ is not a set of representatives, because it has two elements of the coset $2\mathbb{Z}$ and none of $1+2\mathbb{Z}$.

reminder: The cotangent complex of a ring map $A\to B$ is the module of [Kähler differentials](c:kahler-differential) computed on a resolution of $B$.
definition: Let $A\to B$ be a map of commutative rings and let $P_\bullet\to B$ be a resolution of $B$ by simplicial polynomial $A$-algebras. The cotangent complex is $L_{B/A}=\Omega_{P_\bullet/A}\otimes_{P_\bullet}B$, a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) of $B$-modules that is well defined up to quasi-isomorphism, and it is a [derived functor](c:derived-functor) version of the module of [Kähler differentials](c:kahler-differential). Its homology in degree $0$ is $\Omega_{B/A}$.
examples: For a polynomial algebra $B=A[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, the complex $L_{B/A}$ is $\Omega_{B/A}\cong B^n$ in degree $0$.
For $B=A[x]/(f)$ with $f$ a non-zero-divisor, $L_{B/A}$ is the two-term complex $B\xrightarrow{\,f'\,}B$ in degrees $1$ and $0$.

Non-example: $\Omega_{B/A}$ alone is not the cotangent complex, because for $B=k[x]/(x^2)$ with $\operatorname{char}k\ne2$ the homology $H_1(L_{B/k})\cong k$ is non-zero and $\Omega_{B/k}$ cannot see it.

steps: Start with a ring map $A\to B$ and its module $\Omega_{B/A}$ of [Kähler differentials](c:kahler-differential).
Replace $B$ by a resolution $P_\bullet\to B$ by polynomial $A$-algebras, where differentials behave well.
Apply the differentials in each degree to get the complex $L_{B/A}$.
Its homology in degree $0$ is $\Omega_{B/A}$, and its higher homology vanishes when $B$ is smooth over $A$.
links.why: It shows that the cotangent complex keeps the Kähler differentials in degree $0$ and adds higher homology that detects singularities.

reminder: A countable language has only finitely or countably many constant, function and relation symbols.
definition: A [first-order](c:first-order-logic) language $\mathcal{L}$ is countable when its set of symbols, that is its constant symbols, function symbols and relation symbols, is finite or [countable](c:countable-set). Then the set of all formulas of $\mathcal{L}$ is also countable.
examples: The language of rings $\{+,\cdot,-,0,1\}$ is countable.
The language $\{<\}$ of ordered sets is countable.
Non-example: the language of fields with a constant symbol for every real number has $2^{\aleph_0}$ symbols, so it is not countable.

reminder: The counting function of a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) $f$ counts the $a$-points of $f$ in a disc, each weighted by a logarithm.
definition: For a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) $f$ on $\mathbb{C}$ and $a\in\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$, let $n(t,a)$ be the number of $a$-points of $f$ in $|z|\le t$, counted with multiplicity, where the $\infty$-points are the [poles](c:pole-of-a-function). The counting function is $N(r,a)=n(0,a)\log r+\int_0^r\frac{n(t,a)-n(0,a)}{t}\,dt$.
examples: For $f(z)=z^2-1$ and $a=0$, we get $N(r,0)=2\log r$ for $r\ge1$.
For $f(z)=1/z$ and $a=\infty$, we get $N(r,\infty)=\log r$.
For $f(z)=e^z$ and $a=0$, we get $N(r,0)=0$, because $e^z$ has no zeros.
Non-example: the plain count $n(r,a)$ is not $N(r,a)$, because it ignores the logarithmic weight and jumps at each $a$-point.

reminder: The covolume of a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) is the volume of a [fundamental domain](c:fundamental-domain) of the lattice.
definition: For a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ with basis $b_1,\dots,b_n$, the covolume is $|\det(b_1,\dots,b_n)|$, which is the [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) of any [fundamental domain](c:fundamental-domain) of $\Lambda$. For a lattice $\Gamma$ in a [locally compact group](c:locally-compact-group) $G$ with [Haar measure](c:haar-measure), the covolume is the measure of the quotient $G/\Gamma$.
examples: The lattice $\mathbb{Z}^n$ has covolume $1$.
The lattice generated by $(2,0)$ and $(1,3)$ has covolume $|\det\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}|=6$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}+\sqrt2\,\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}$ is dense, not discrete, so it is not a lattice and has no covolume.

reminder: The cross ratio of four points on a [projective line](c:projective-line) is a number that every [projective transformation](c:projective-transformation) keeps unchanged.
definition: For four distinct points $z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4$ of a [projective line](c:projective-line) over a [field](c:field), the cross ratio is $(z_1,z_2;z_3,z_4)=\dfrac{(z_1-z_3)(z_2-z_4)}{(z_2-z_3)(z_1-z_4)}$, with the usual rule when a point is $\infty$. It does not change when one [projective transformation](c:projective-transformation) acts on all four points; other books order the points differently.
examples: $(0,1;2,3)=\frac{(-2)(-2)}{(-1)(-3)}=\frac43$, and the map $x\mapsto2x+5$ gives the same value for the images $5,7,9,11$.
$(0,\infty;1,-1)=-1$, a harmonic quadruple.
Non-example: the simple ratio $(z_3-z_1)/(z_2-z_1)$ of three points is not a cross ratio, because $x\mapsto1/x$ changes its value on $1,2,3$ from $2$ to $4/3$.

reminder: The $n$-cube is the product of $n$ unit intervals, and it has $2^n$ vertices.
definition: The $n$-dimensional cube, or $n$-cube, is the product $[0,1]^n\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ of $n$ copies of the [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[0,1]$ in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), up to scaling and moving. Its vertices are the points with every coordinate $0$ or $1$, and its faces come from fixing some coordinates to $0$ or $1$.
examples: The $2$-cube is the unit square, and the $3$-cube has $8$ vertices, $12$ edges and $6$ faces.
The $n$-cube has $2^n$ vertices and $2n$ facets.
Non-example: the box $[0,1]\times[0,2]\times[0,3]$ is not a cube, because its sides have different lengths.

steps: The cube $[0,1]^n$ is the intersection of the $2n$ closed half-spaces $x_i\ge0$ and $x_i\le1$.
This intersection is bounded.
So the cube is a bounded intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces, which is a [convex polytope](c:convex-polytope).
links.why: It shows that results about convex polytopes, such as the face structure, apply to cubes.

reminder: The cup product multiplies [cohomology](c:cohomology) classes of degrees $p$ and $q$ to give a class of degree $p+q$.
definition: The cup product is a bilinear map $H^p(X;R)\times H^q(X;R)\to H^{p+q}(X;R)$ that makes $H^*(X;R)$ a graded-commutative [cohomology ring](c:cohomology-ring). On singular [cochains](c:cochain) it is $(\alpha\cup\beta)(\sigma)=\alpha(\sigma|_{[v_0,\dots,v_p]})\,\beta(\sigma|_{[v_p,\dots,v_{p+q}]})$ for a singular $(p+q)$-simplex $\sigma$ with vertices $v_0,\dots,v_{p+q}$.
examples: $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^n;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^{n+1})$ with $|x|=2$, where the cup product is the product of polynomials.
On the torus $T^2$, for generators $a,b$ of $H^1$, the product $a\cup b$ generates $H^2$.
In de Rham cohomology, the cup product is induced by the wedge product of differential forms.
Non-example: the pointwise product $(\alpha\cdot\beta)(\sigma)=\alpha(\sigma)\beta(\sigma)$ needs $p=q$ and gives a cochain of degree $p$, not $p+q$, so it is not the cup product.

reminder: The curl of a [vector field](c:vector-field) in three dimensions measures its local rotation and is again a vector field.
definition: For a [vector field](c:vector-field) $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, the curl is $\nabla\times v=(\partial_2v_3-\partial_3v_2,\ \partial_3v_1-\partial_1v_3,\ \partial_1v_2-\partial_2v_1)$, with [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) $\partial_i$. On an oriented Riemannian 3-manifold, the curl is the vector field $\operatorname{curl}v=\star\,d(v^\flat)$.
examples: The field $v=(-y,x,0)$ has curl $(0,0,2)$.
Every gradient field $v=\nabla f$ has curl $0$.
Non-example: the divergence $\partial_1v_1+\partial_2v_2+\partial_3v_3$ is a scalar function, not a vector field, so it is not the curl.

steps: Turn $v$ into the 1-form $v^\flat=v_1\,dx+v_2\,dy+v_3\,dz$.
Apply the [de Rham differential](c:de-rham-differential) $d$ to get a 2-form.
Apply the Hodge star, which turns 2-forms into 1-forms in dimension $3$.
Raise the index to get a vector field; the result is $\nabla\times v$.
links.why:
It shows that the curl is the exterior derivative in dimension $3$, so $\operatorname{curl}
abla f=0$ follows from $d^2=0$.

reminder: A smooth curve in a manifold $X$ is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) from an [interval](c:interval) of the real line to $X$.
definition: A smooth curve in a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $X$ is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $\gamma:I\to X$ from an [interval](c:interval) $I\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. It has a velocity vector $\gamma'(t)$ in the tangent space at $\gamma(t)$ for each $t$, and it is regular when $\gamma'(t)\ne0$ for all $t$.
examples: The map $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a smooth curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$ that runs around the unit circle.
The map $\gamma(t)=(t,t^2)$ is a smooth curve whose image is a parabola.
Non-example: $\gamma(t)=(t,|t|)$ is continuous, but it is not smooth at $t=0$, so it is not a smooth curve.

steps: Take a smooth curve $\gamma$ in a Riemannian manifold with the Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$.
Add the condition that the acceleration vanishes: $\nabla_{\gamma'}\gamma'=0$.
Then $\gamma$ is a [geodesic](c:geodesic).
links.why: It shows that a geodesic is a smooth curve with zero acceleration.

reminder: A cycle is a closed walk that repeats no edge and no vertex, except that it ends where it starts.
definition: In a [graph](c:graph), a cycle at a [vertex](c:vertex) $u$ is a closed walk $u=v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k=u$ in which no [edge](c:edge) repeats and the vertices $v_0,\dots,v_{k-1}$ are distinct. Its length $k$ is at least $3$, and the cycle with its edges forms a connected subgraph in which every vertex has degree $2$.
examples: A triangle $a,b,c,a$ in any graph is a cycle of length $3$.
In the complete graph $K_4$, there are cycles of length $3$ and of length $4$.
Non-example: the closed walk $u,v,u$ uses the same edge twice, so it is not a cycle.
Non-example: the walk $a,b,c,a,d,e,a$ visits $a$ three times, so it is not a cycle.

reminder: The cycle index of a group of permutations is the average of the cycle-type monomials of its elements.
definition: Let $G$ be a group of [permutations](c:permutation) of an $n$-element set, and let $c_k(g)$ be the number of [cycles](c:cycle-of-a-permutation) of length $k$ of $g\in G$. The cycle index of the [group](c:group) $G$ is the [polynomial](c:polynomial) $Z(G)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\prod_{k=1}^{n}x_k^{c_k(g)}$ in $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
examples: For the rotation group of a square acting on its $4$ corners, $Z(C_4)=\frac14(x_1^4+x_2^2+2x_4)$.
Non-example: the sum $\sum_g\prod_kx_k^{c_k(g)}$ without the factor $1/|G|$ is not the cycle index, because its coefficients add up to $|G|$ and not to $1$.

reminder: A cycle of a [permutation](c:permutation) is an [orbit](c:orbit) of the points under repeated application of the permutation.
definition: Let $\sigma$ be a [permutation](c:permutation) of a set $X$. A cycle of $\sigma$ is an [orbit](c:orbit) of the [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) $\langle\sigma\rangle$ acting on $X$, listed in the order $x,\sigma(x),\sigma^2(x),\dots$, and its length is the size of the orbit. Every point lies in exactly one cycle, and a fixed point is a cycle of length $1$.
examples: The permutation $\sigma=(1\,3\,2)(4\,5)$ of $\{1,\dots,6\}$ has the cycles $(1\,3\,2)$, $(4\,5)$ and $(6)$.
The identity of an $n$-element set has $n$ cycles of length $1$.
Non-example: for $\sigma=(1\,2\,3)(4\,5)$ the set $\{1,4\}$ is not a cycle, because it meets two different orbits.

reminder: Cyclic homology of an algebra is the homology of the Hochschild complex with tensor factors identified up to cyclic rotation.
definition: Let $A$ be an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) over a commutative ring $k$ that contains $\mathbb{Q}$. On $C_n(A)=A^{\otimes(n+1)}$, let $t(a_0\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n)=(-1)^na_n\otimes a_0\otimes\cdots\otimes a_{n-1}$, and let $b$ be the boundary of [Hochschild homology](c:hochschild-homology). The cyclic homology $HC_n(A)$ is the homology of the quotient [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $(C_*(A)/(1-t),\,b)$; for a general $k$ one takes the total complex of Connes' bicomplex.
examples: $HC_0(A)=A/[A,A]$ for every algebra $A$.
For a field $k$ of characteristic $0$, $HC_n(k)=k$ for even $n$ and $HC_n(k)=0$ for odd $n$.
Non-example: Hochschild homology is not cyclic homology, because $HH_n(k)=0$ for $n>0$ while $HC_{2m}(k)=k$.

reminder: A [permutation](c:permutation) of a finite set is cyclic when one [cycle](c:cycle-of-a-permutation) of it contains every point.
definition: A [permutation](c:permutation) $\sigma$ of a [finite set](c:finite-set) $X$ is cyclic when the [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) $\langle\sigma\rangle$ acts [transitively](c:transitive-action) on $X$, that is, for all $x,y\in X$ some power satisfies $\sigma^m(x)=y$. Equivalently, $\sigma$ has exactly one cycle, of length $|X|$.
examples: The permutation $(1\,2\,3\,4)$ of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is cyclic.
The shift $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb{Z}/n$ is cyclic.
Non-example: $(1\,2)(3\,4)$ on $\{1,2,3,4\}$ has the two orbits $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$, so $1$ never reaches $3$ and the permutation is not cyclic.

steps: Take a cyclic permutation $\sigma$ of $X$, which is a bijection from $X$ to $X$.
So $\sigma$ is a [permutation](c:permutation) of $X$.
The cyclic case adds one condition: the group generated by $\sigma$ acts transitively on $X$.
links.why: It shows that a cyclic permutation is a permutation with a single orbit.
